Kalyani from room 214 has been in the common room past two most nights this month, laptop open, chai flask beside her. Her roommate says she misses the nine o'clock lecture twice a week. Today she snapped at the mess staff over cold rice, then sat on the stairs looking flat rather than angry. I asked if she was all right. She said she felt anxious all the time and didn't know why; she thought she just needed more motivation. I asked when she last slept a full night. She laughed, then stopped laughing. We agreed on a small trial: lights off by 12:30 for one week, chai only before five, and a walk to breakfast. I'll check in with her on Monday.

Sunday night
Weird week. Monday to Thursday I was up till three finishing the fest posters, living on chai from the gate stall. Skipped two labs. On Friday I cried because Tanuja borrowed my charger without asking. Over a charger! Then I felt nothing at all for a whole day, like someone had turned my colour down.
Today I slept eleven hours by accident and woke up fine. Happy, even. Tanuja pointed out, gently, that I'm always "dramatic" on Fridays, after the late nights. Rude but true.
So, an experiment. Bed by 12:30 on weeknights, phone on the other side of the room, no chai after dinner. Not a new planner, not another productivity video. Just sleep. Let's see if Friday Keerthana is nicer.

Writing this instead of saying it, because I keep chickening out at 2 am.
For the last three weeks your lamp and calls have gone on till around two, and I've been waking up wrecked. I'll be honest: I've been slamming my cupboard in the mornings and leaving sticky notes that were more sarcastic than helpful. That isn't fair to you either, and I'm sorry.

Can we talk about it over dinner tonight? I'd rather sort it now than turn into roommates who don't speak.

passage: Honestly? I didn't say anything for two months. That was the mistake. I'm Charu, second year, and my roommate Uday was the nicest night owl you could meet. He gamed with headphones till three, but the keyboard went clack-clack-clack like rain on a tin roof. I lay there doing maths in my head: if I fall asleep now, I get four hours. By November I was banging my water bottle on the desk in the mornings and answering him in single words. He had no idea why. One night I just said it: "Uday, the keyboard's killing me. Could you use a quieter one after twelve, or play in the lounge?" He looked shocked, then said, "Why didn't you tell me in August?" We bought a rubber keyboard cover together that weekend. Two months of sulking, fixed in one sentence.

qa.q: What did Charu and Uday buy together?
qa.a: A rubber keyboard cover.

qa.a: Charu felt frustrated and resentful, counting the few hours of sleep left, which came out as bottle-banging and single-word answers.

qa.a: It named the exact problem and offered two options, a quieter keyboard after twelve or the lounge, so fixing it felt easy.

qa.q: How did Uday experience the months of silence?
qa.a: Uday had no idea what was wrong and was shocked to learn the reason, wishing Charu had spoken in August.

Fifth night this week under five hours. I used to be proud of that. The team calls me the machine.
Today the machine sent the client the wrong spreadsheet, the one full of our internal comments. Suraj caught it before they opened it, thank God. Then in the 4 pm meeting I snapped at Suraj when he asked a simple question, and the whole room went quiet. My fourth coffee of the day was in my hand.
On the metro home I did the maths. Longest hours in the team, most mistakes this month. The hours aren't making me better. They're making me slower and meaner.

Jyoti has looked worn out for about six weeks. Today she told me she lies awake most nights, even though she has cut screens at night, kept a fixed wake time and darkened her room. She said she has started dreading bedtime and feels low most mornings. Her plan was to "just push through till the project ends". I told her, gently, that this sounded like something a doctor should hear about, not something to push through. She booked an appointment with her doctor for Friday, and I've cleared her afternoon so she can go. She asked me not to share details with the team, and I won't. I'll ask how she is next week, without pressing.
Sumit

Night 23 of this. 2:10 am.
I've done everything the articles say. Same wake-up at 6:30, even on Sundays. Phone in the kitchen. Blackout curtains. Warm milk. And still I lie here with my heart going fast, making lists of everything that could go wrong at work.
Vidya called tonight and asked how I was. I said fine. She said, "You've said 'fine' in that voice for weeks." Then I cried on the phone for ten minutes, which probably answers it.
She made me promise to book a doctor tomorrow and not wait and see. I've stuck a note on the mirror: CALL CLINIC 9 AM. I'll keep the habits too; Vidya says they'll help with whatever the doctor suggests.
I feel stupid needing help with sleep. But three weeks of this isn't stupid. It's just too long.
Aditi

Kalyani snapped at me today, and I spent three hours sulking about it. We'd been shifting her stuff to the new PG since morning, no breakfast, no lunch, just boxes.
